items.title: US data brokers are selling half a billion dollars in RL training environments to Chinese AI labs
items.desc: US data brokers like Mercor, Surge AI, and AfterQuery are selling roughly half a billion dollars' worth of AI training data to Chinese labs, according to a ChinaTalk investigation. That includes the same RL environments previously built for OpenAI or Anthropic. At least nine firms are involved, and export controls barely apply. The article US data brokers are selling half a billion dollars in RL training environments to Chinese AI labs appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: American data brokers sell so-called RL environments to Chinese AI labs, helping them save compute during model development. A ChinaTalk investigation identifies at least nine companies involved. American data firms like Mercor, Surge AI, AfterQuery, and Turing are selling roughly half a billion dollars' worth of training data to Chinese AI labs, according to an investigation by ChinaTalk . Some of that data takes the form of reinforcement learning environments, which are simulated worlds where AI models are trained on specific tasks like coding, financial analysis, or office work. Chinese labs deliberately buy the same products previously sold to Anthropic or OpenAI, the report says. That way, they already know the data works and can skip costly in-house development and wasted training runs. Because Chinese chips suffer from acute memory bottlenecks, those savings are particularly valuable for labs there. Ad There is also the issue of distillation. Chinese labs use powerful US models like GPT or Claude as "teachers," using their outputs as training examples. Combined with purchased RL environments, this creates a two-pronged advantage that lets Chinese labs close the gap with less compute of their own. Ad The authors identified at least nine US data firms selling to Chinese customers. AfterQuery reportedly draws a significant share of its annual recurring revenue from Chinese customers. ChinaTalk points to Forbes reports of about $100 million in ARR but could not independently verify the sales. Surge AI openly advertises on its website that its products are "built by the same experts behind our frontier-lab work." The deals also run through offshore structures. ByteDance maintains procurement offices in Singapore and San Jose. Ad These business relationships came to light through a combination of anonymous sources and sloppy operational security among subcontractors, according to ChinaTalk. The US data firms outsource much of the actual RL environment creation and data curation to low-paid workers in developing countries, especially India. Those subcontractors then sometimes post client names on LinkedIn or in résumés, even though they are supposed to use only code names. Export controls barely apply because RL environments remain largely unregulated. Domains with dual-use potential pose particular risks: Coding environments improve software development but can also sharpen offensive cyber capabilities. Biology environments could improve gene synthesis capabilities and potentially enhance bioweapons-relevant applications. The ChinaTalk authors argue that the Bureau of Industry and Security should subject these dual-use environments to existing export controls. Ad At the same time, the authors stress that these relationships are not apocalyptic. By piggybacking on US work, Chinese labs still trail their US peers by at least a few months as a structural matter. Sensitive environments in areas like biology, chemistry, cybersecurity, chip design, and investment banking are increasingly being built in-house at American frontier companies, the authors say. items.title: Enterprise sales push OpenAI's quarterly revenue to $10 billion, though it still trails Anthropic
items.desc: OpenAI grew its quarterly revenue 50 percent to $10 billion but is still burning more cash than it brings in. Adjusted operating losses climbed to $10.9 billion, while rival Anthropic operates far more efficiently on $17 billion in revenue. To close the gap, OpenAI is now fueling a price war for enterprise customers. The article Enterprise sales push OpenAI's quarterly revenue to $10 billion, though it still trails Anthropic appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: OpenAI posts a massive Q3 revenue jump, driven by new AI models and enterprise customers. But operating losses keep growing, while rival Anthropic operates far more efficiently ahead of its IPO. According to reports from the Wall Street Journal and The Information , OpenAI grew its revenue by about 50 percent quarter over quarter in Q3 to $10 billion. In Q2, revenue had grown by just 17 to 18 percent . A year earlier, the company brought in $3.9 billion. Despite tripling revenue within a year, adjusted operating losses rose slightly in Q3 from $10.1 billion to $10.9 billion. That figure doesn't include stock-based compensation, which climbed to $2.6 billion. The adjusted operating margin did improve, going from negative 150 percent in Q2 to negative 109 percent. A year earlier it was negative 97 percent. Ad That puts OpenAI behind industry leader Anthropic, which plans its IPO next week. The Claude developer already overtook OpenAI on revenue in Q2 and even posted a small operating profit at the time. In Q3, Anthropic grew revenue 47 percent to $17 billion, while its operating loss including stock compensation came to just $567 million. Ad The efficiency gap comes down to business models. Anthropic focuses heavily on enterprise customers and successful tools like Claude Code and the Claude Cowork agent. OpenAI, by contrast, funds broad research into robotics and runs an expensive consumer business. To catch up in the enterprise market, OpenAI reshuffled its priorities earlier this year. The company discontinued projects like a video app, put more resources into its coding tool Codex , and hired Dali Rajic as its new head of sales. At the same time, OpenAI cut prices on new models. Ad Third-party data showed companies seeking cheaper alternatives to Claude, which boosted API sales. OpenAI president Greg Brockman called it an incredible revenue turning point and pointed to major customers like JPMorgan Chase. The enterprise business doubled in Q3 and now accounts for the bulk of revenue, Brockman said. The consumer side is growing too. ChatGPT now has 1.2 billion weekly active users, with 100 million paying subscribers after 22 million new sign-ups. On top of that, the new ChatGPT ad product hit an annualized revenue run rate of $1 billion in August. Ad Both competitors are feeling the recent tech sell-off in the financial markets. OpenAI is targeting an IPO next year and is currently raising fresh capital at a $1.25 trillion valuation , but has so far raised less than half of the planned $30 billion. Anthropic also had to cut its IPO valuation target significantly. items.title: Nvidia's model GR00T 2 watches humans on video, then imagines itself as the robot
items.desc: Nvidia's new AI model GR00T 2 is designed to teach robots new tasks without laborious teleoperation. Instead, the system transfers human hand movements from videos to robotic arms, trained on about 400,000 hours of video footage. Success rates still vary widely, though, ranging from 10 to 80 percent depending on the task. The article Nvidia's model GR00T 2 watches humans on video, then imagines itself as the robot appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: Nvidia's model GR00T 2 watches humans on video, then imagines itself as the robot Maximilian Schreiner View the LinkedIn Profile of Maximilian Schreiner Nov 10, 2026 Nvidia To teach robots new tasks, humans usually have to laboriously teleoperate them during training. Nvidia's new AI model GR00T 2 is designed to cut that effort by transferring human movements from videos to robotic arms. To train a robot for new tasks, engineers usually spend hours remotely controlling the machines. This so-called teleoperation is expensive, slow, and needs its own data for every robot model. In a new research report on GR00T 2 , Nvidia introduces a new AI foundation model designed to shorten this process. Unlike previous approaches, including its predecessor GR00T 1, GR00T 2 doesn't translate camera images and language commands directly into motor movements. Nvidia says the software works as what the company calls a world-action model. It simultaneously calculates the next movement and a short video of the immediate future. The system predicts how the camera image should change when a robotic arm picks up an object, for example. This video prediction should let the model transfer movement sequences between different robot form factors. Nvidia trained the system on a cluster with more than a thousand GB300 chips, including about 400,000 hours of video footage showing people performing various tasks while wearing head-mounted cameras. To then teach a robot a new task, the researchers say it should be enough for a person to demonstrate the steps using data gloves, specialized hand grippers, or a finger exoskeleton. When these recordings are combined during training with general motion data from the target robot, the AI generates the robotic arm instead of the human arm in its video prediction and derives the matching control commands from that. In lab tests, a robot with five-fingered hands was able to light a match, slice a banana, or toss packages onto a conveyor belt this way, without having been teleoperated for those specific tasks. Success rates varied between 10 and 80 percent depending on the task. From a single video of a human hand movement, the system also learned to hammer nails by way of a computer simulation. For 50 selected tasks where the model already performed well after just a few examples, less than three minutes of conventional training was enough to raise the success rate from 40 to 95 percent. For longer assembly work, Nvidia pairs the system with a higher-level AI language model like OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra. While GR00T 2 handles the gripping movements, the language model breaks the task into individual steps, color-codes grip points in the camera image, and launches helper routines when a part falls off. When the researchers placed loose parts for toy models on a table in no particular order, the combined system assembled them in at least 97 percent of trials. Without the corrective language model and additional fine-tuning, the toy car assembly succeeded in only 23 out of 100 attempts. items.full: US corporate AI spending hit a new high in October 2026, but growth was modest. The Ramp AI Index, which tracks AI spending among business customers of financial services provider Ramp, showed a 1.65 percent increase month over month. The heaviest AI users spent somewhat more, according to Ramp . The top one percent of companies by AI spending paid a median of $10,200 per employee per month, up nine percent. A typical company, by contrast, spent just $16.32, a slight increase of less than a dollar from the previous month. Ad Ramp's data reflects market trends but isn't necessarily representative. The index draws on payment data from more than 85,000 US companies, though free AI tools and usage through personal accounts may be missing from the figures. Ad According to Ramp, separate metrics on token volume and spending come only from companies using Ramp Token Spend Management and aren't representative of overall AI spending on the platform. The customer base skews growth-oriented, tech-savvy, and larger than US businesses overall, so AI adoption is likely overstated. Business customers' spending on OpenAI grew 2.1 percent month over month, compared with just 0.5 percent for Anthropic. According to Ramp chief economist Ara Kharazian, the structural risks he identified in his earlier analysis persist. One percent of companies drive 80 percent of revenue for OpenAI and Anthropic. Ad That top tier is mostly venture-backed firms in tech, finance, and technical services. Outside those sectors, AI adoption is barely spreading. Prices are falling at the same time. The average price per million processed text tokens dropped 21 percent last month, according to Ramp. Usage volume is growing faster than spending, so AI keeps getting cheaper, driven by competitive pressure between OpenAI and Anthropic along with open-weight models from China. Ad SpacexSI also grew strongly at 2.2 percent, making it the fastest-growing software company in Ramp's entire dataset. That likely says more about bias in Ramp's data than about any big win for Grok. The company's models aren't particularly noteworthy, and the growth is probably driven by the coding tool Cursor, which belongs to SpacexSI . On Ramp, the company holds a 6.3 percent market share, a figure that most likely doesn't reflect the broader market. Anthropic reached 44.8 percent adoption, up 1.1 percentage points, while OpenAI held steady at 40.6 percent. Overall adoption of AI services rose to 56.8 percent. Software development teams accounted for 72 percent of all tracked AI spending in October, but their spending has declined from summer highs. Customer support and customer success departments saw the strongest growth, with their share of AI spending climbing from 0.8 percent in June to 13.3 percent in October, possibly driven by AI chatbots in customer service. Leadership teams also spent slightly more. But customer support is nowhere near matching the rapid growth development teams posted earlier this year, Kharazian writes. items.title: Google Deepmind's AlphaProof Code verified Signal's cryptographic core in four weeks instead of years
items.desc: Google Deepmind's AlphaProof Code mathematically verified Signal's cryptographic core code in four weeks, a process that typically takes years. AI agents powered by Gemini Carbon wrote more than six million lines of proof code and flagged only about one percent for human review. Deepmind plans to extend the method to critical infrastructure like power grids and medical devices. The article Google Deepmind's AlphaProof Code verified Signal's cryptographic core in four weeks instead of years appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: Google Deepmind has unveiled AlphaProof Code, an AI system that mathematically proves software meets its security specs without errors. Researchers demonstrated the technology on Signal's encryption protocol, completing in four weeks work that typically takes years. Earlier verification efforts stopped at the theoretical design stage, according to a blog post by DeepMind researchers Pushmeet Kohli and Swarat Chaudhuri. AlphaProof Code verified the actual cryptographic core code running on users' devices. After experts defined formal security requirements, AI agents built on Gemini Carbon wrote over six million lines in the Lean proof language, flagging roughly one percent of the codebase for human review. Two bugs planted deliberately for testing were caught immediately. Signal CTO Ehren Kret says the approach strengthens trust in data privacy as AI threats grow. DeepMind plans to extend the method to power grids and medical devices through systems like CodeMender . items.full: Anthropic claims it has broken free of its Nvidia dependence with a multi-chip strategy. The company says it ported its own AI model, Claude, to AMD GPUs in just three days, with almost no human intervention. Nvidia's biggest competitive edge is the combination of hardware and software, specifically CUDA, the software ecosystem that locks developers into Nvidia chips. Porting AI models to other chip architectures takes so much effort that many companies won't even try. Anthropic now claims in an investor presentation that it has solved this problem using AI itself. According to Tom Brown, co-founder and Chief Compute Officer at Anthropic, the company now trains and runs Claude on all four major chip families. Anthropic made an "unconventional bet" on a multi-chip strategy early on, at a time when most of the industry considered the effort not worth it. Each chip needs its own custom software and inference stack, which is expensive and time-consuming. But Anthropic has been investing in this work for years and has since become "incredibly good" at it, Brown says. Ad The company's most concrete test came with AMD GPUs. Until now, bringing up a new chip platform kept dozens of engineers busy for months. This year, Anthropic used AMD GPUs for the first time and let its own frontier model, Mythos, do the work. According to Anthropic, Claude was running on AMD after just three days, with almost no human intervention. The model ported or wrote nearly 100 percent of the kernels itself. Ad If these figures are accurate, the software overhead, long considered Nvidia's strongest competitive advantage, would shrink dramatically because of AI. Companies could switch more easily between chip providers and pick the most affordable or readily available option. In a compute market where supply is tight, a multi-chip approach lets companies focus on the best price-performance ratio, regardless of the vendor. Some chips are better for training, while others are better for inference. And because of its dominance in the AI chip market, Nvidia currently enjoys a margin of more than 70 percent, which is unusually high for hardware. Ad Anthropic treats compute from different vendors, chip architectures, and locations as one interchangeable pool. The company says it gets more out of every dollar of compute than any other frontier AI lab. Beyond its multi-chip strategy, Anthropic relies on what it calls compute multipliers, research breakthroughs that squeeze more performance from the same physical computing capacity. According to Anthropic, these multipliers build on one another so that each new breakthrough amplifies the effect of the previous one. Ad Eventually, Claude should be able to discover such compute multipliers on its own. That would amount to recursive self-improvement, a concept that's intensely debated in AI research but hasn't been proven yet . Ad Anthropic is also building its own data center capacity through the "Anthropic Direct" program. Instead of buying computing power only as a cloud service, the company leases chips and operates them in purpose-built data centers. The goal is to reduce total cost of ownership. items.title: Should You Actually Add AI To That? A Four-Question Audit For Product Teams
items.desc: An AI feature can save users time on a task, only for them to spend it checking the results. This practical audit helps product teams decide where AI earns its place and what users need to verify its output.
items.full: About The Author Victor Yocco, PhD, is a UX Researcher with a focus on AI and the author of Designing Agentic AI Experiences (CRC Press, 2026), Design for the Mind (Manning, … More about Victor ↬ Weekly tips on front-end & UX . Trusted by 182,000+ folks. How To Measure UX and Design Impact, 8h video + UX training Meet AI 2027 Conference, December 1, 2026. Celebrating 10 million developers Smart Interface Design Patterns, 45 lessons + UX training Advertise on Smashing Magazine An AI feature can save users time on a task, only for them to spend it checking the results. This practical audit helps product teams decide where AI earns its place and what users need to verify its output. A product team at a large health insurer wants to add AI that writes the full written determination for benefits appeals specialists. The technology works as specified. However, the specialists stop using it, and the ones who keep using it take longer on each case than the ones who ignore it. A short evaluation with the specialists surfaces the problem fast: reading an AI-written determination carefully enough to sign it takes about as long as writing one, and the specialist also has to check for mistakes they would never have made themselves. The feature adds work to a task these people had already mastered. Rescoping the release fixes it. A second version surfaces the policy provisions and prior decisions relevant to each appeal and leaves the writing to the specialist. The search step disappears, review time drops, and the part of the job the specialist is good at stays where it was. The technology is identical in both versions, and the difference is which part of the task the AI handles. Every interface change costs the user something before it pays anything back. They have to rebuild their picture of how the tool works, learn where things are now, and decide how far to trust what the AI hands them. Nelson Cowan’s review of working memory research (2001) put the limit at about four items held in mind at once. All three of those jobs draw on the same small supply. An AI feature in an enterprise software setting requires more from the user than a redesigned menu, because it changes what they do all day. Hand the synthesis to an AI and the user becomes a checker. Give it the recommendation too, and the job shrinks to signing off. Either change costs user attention, and for people whose training is their standing at work, either one can feel like a demotion. For example, in one study, Sophia Ackerhans (2025) and colleagues found that physicians asked to sign AI-assisted decisions reported a more serious threat to their professional identity, and explanations of the AI’s reasoning raised both trust and that threat together. We can call that the break-even line . Returns to users come in three forms: For example, an AI-powered fraud screening tool shows the errors-caught form at work, since the analyst reviews flags they would never have raised themselves, which costs attention, and the catch rate pays for it. items.title: Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia CEO after espionage scandal wipes out $1.4 trillion in market value
items.desc: Jensen Huang resigned as CEO, president, and board member of Nvidia effective immediately, according to a statement on November 12, 2026. The article Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia CEO after espionage scandal wipes out $1.4 trillion in market value appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: Jensen Huang resigned as CEO, president, and board member of Nvidia effective immediately, according to a statement on November 12, 2026. The move came after the Wall Street Journal reported that the board was planning to fire Huang following revelations about two extramarital affairs, one of them with a suspected Chinese spy . Since a New York Times report on October 29 about possible ties to Chinese intelligence, Nvidia has shed roughly $1.4 trillion in market value. CFO Colette Kress is taking over on an interim basis while the board searches for a permanent successor. Harvey C. Jones will serve as the first independent board chair and stressed that business operations continue without disruption. Replacing Huang will be difficult because Nvidia was built entirely around him. He secured the company's market position through a complex web of alliances with financiers and roughly $300 billion in guarantees for smaller customers. His departure could unravel that structure, which he used to keep major tech rivals at bay and support large parts of the AI industry. Ad Major customers like Microsoft, Amazon, and Alphabet, along with AI labs like OpenAI and Anthropic, depend heavily on Nvidia's chips, but the company's 75 percent profit margin is pushing them to develop their own, cheaper alternatives. Huang also left no clear succession plan, with more than 60 employees reporting directly to him, leaving both internal and external candidates starting from a weakened position. items.title: Beyond 12 Columns: Designing Layouts With Personality
items.desc: Too many websites look alike. They use familiar layouts, repeat the same patterns, and often leave little impression once you’ve moved on. Andy Clarke explores how understanding a company’s story can lead to more distinctive designs, using modular and compound grids to create layouts with character. Beyond 12 Columns: Designing Layouts With Personality originally handwritten and published with love on CSS-Tricks . You should really get the newsletter as well.
items.full: NVIDIA L4 GPUs. 5-second cold starts. Scale to zero when idle. When I started designing websites thirty years ago, David Siegel had just published Creating Killer Web Sites , the book that popularised HTML tables and spacer GIFs for laying out web pages. CSS eventually gave us more control over layouts through floats and positioning. Neither was intended for page layout, and inconsistent browser behaviour could make using them frustrating. Still, that didn’t stop me and a generation of other designers from using floats and positioning. When CSS frameworks began providing ready-made grid systems, things got a little easier. Blueprint CSS ) offered a 24-column grid, while Nathan Smith’s 960 Grid System offered 12- and 16-column options. These frameworks gave designers and developers a shared structure, making layout planning and implementation considerably easier. Twelve-column grids weren’t invented in the 2000s. Graphic designers had used column-based and modular grids for decades, and twelve is a convenient number because you don’t need to be a maths genius to divide it into halves, thirds, and quarters to create the 2-up, 3-up, and 4-up components we see everywhere online. Frameworks like Bootstrap and Foundation followed, helping establish twelve-column grids as the de facto standard for page layouts. I get why that happened. But somewhere along the way, one layout option became the default starting point for almost everything. CSS Grid changed what’s possible for page layouts, but I still see designers start by dividing a page into twelve equal columns, then deciding how to fit their content into them. The designs they end up with might be perfectly fine, but they can also look remarkably similar. Still, I don’t think twelve-column grids themselves are the problem. It’s reaching for a familiar solution before considering what makes the company I’m designing for distinctive and what its website needs to communicate. So what happens when I start with those questions instead? Every company has a story worth telling Before I decide how many columns a layout needs, I want to understand the company I’m designing for. What makes it different from its competitors? What does it want people to remember? Does it have a personality that could influence how its website looks and feels? These questions matter because a layout does more than arrange content. The size, position, and relationships between elements influence how people experience a website. A restrained, orderly composition can communicate something very different from one that’s full of energy and movement. So to demonstrate what I mean, I’ll use Wheelman. It’s a fictional company I invented for my book, Standout Designs for the Web . Pre-orders for Standout Designs for the Web are now open in the CSS-Tricks store. Wheelman provides products and services for getaway drivers, including legal advice, robbery insurance, and an online shop selling break-in essentials. It also publishes a magazine with advice, news, and stories about life behind the wheel. Wheelman isn’t an ordinary company, so why should its website look like an everyday collection of components? It takes its business serious
